title: Capt. Abraham Lincoln on Long Run
summary: Capt. Abraham Lincoln, the president’s grandfather, settled on Long Run in Jefferson County in 1782 and was killed there while planting corn in May 1786.
bodyMarkdown:
Long before anyone in Kentucky had heard of the sixteenth president, his grandfather was clearing land in Jefferson County. [Capt. Abraham Lincoln](/people/#abraham-lincoln-capt) was a Virginia militia officer and tanner from the Augusta and Rockingham country of the Shenandoah Valley. He bought rich land near Hughes' Station, in the Floyd's Fork and Long Run country east of the Falls of the Ohio, and in 1782 he moved his family west.

Lincoln had seen frontier war before. In 1778 his militia company [marched to the Ohio frontier](https://grokipedia.com/page/Abraham_Lincoln_(captain)) with the Continental push toward British Detroit and helped build Fort Laurens and Fort McIntosh through a hard winter.

In Kentucky the danger was close. Raids were frequent enough that the family lived inside Hughes' Station, about half a mile from their cabin, rather than on the farm itself, according to the [National Register nomination](https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/b3371983-d150-463e-b2d4-79764877332b) for the church that later rose on the Lincoln land.

In May 1786 Lincoln was planting corn with his sons Mordecai, Josiah, and young Thomas when he was shot from the timber. Mordecai, the eldest, ran for a rifle at a nearby cabin. Josiah ran to the station for help. A warrior came out of the woods toward Thomas, and Mordecai killed him before the boy could be carried off.

The widow soon moved the family to what is now Washington County. Thomas grew up there, and his son, the future president, later wrote that this story was "more strongly than all others imprinted" on his memory. A frontier killing in a Jefferson County cornfield became part of the Lincoln family memory, and through it part of the nation's.

By tradition the family's abandoned cabin became the first meeting place of the Long Run Baptist congregation. A stone church replaced it in 1797 and a brick one in 1844, said to reuse the older masonry. That building burned on December 24, 1960, and its four walls still stand as ruins. Lincoln's grandson's wife, [Mary Todd Lincoln](/people/#mary-todd-lincoln), came from the Lexington Todds, so the family's Kentucky roots ran deep on both sides.

## Kentucky today

State historical marker #101, "Abraham Lincoln," stands on US 60 about a mile east of Eastwood in eastern Louisville. It points two miles northeast to the killing ground and to Long Run Baptist Church, which stands on the Lincoln land grant. The church ruins and Long Run Cemetery, on Old Stage Coach Road, hold a memorial stone to "Abraham Linkhorn"; the original grave is unmarked.
